title: Fear, Possessions, Watchfulness, and the Signs of the Time
summary: Before a vast crowd, Jesus warns his disciples against hypocrisy and tells them to fear God rather than those who can only kill the body, trusting the Father who counts every hair. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, he warns against greed with the parable of the rich fool and tells disciples not to worry but to seek God's kingdom and store treasure in heaven. He calls them to be ready for the Son of Man's return, speaks of the fire and baptism he must undergo, and urges the crowds to read the present time.
story: Chapter 11 ended with the scribes and Pharisees plotting to catch Jesus. Now, surrounded by thousands, he prepares his disciples for a hostile world. The chapter moves outward in a series of warnings. Opposition may bring death, but the Father cares for his own. Wealth promises security, but death can come tonight. The master is coming back, but the delay tempts servants to grow careless. Jesus himself faces a baptism of suffering, and his coming will divide even families. The road to Jerusalem is also the road toward judgment and decision.
historical:
Luke's first readers, probably living decades after Jesus' ministry, knew what it was to be brought before synagogues, rulers, and authorities (verse 11); Acts tells of apostles tried before the Sanhedrin, Roman governors, and a Herodian king. The promise that the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say was not abstract to them.

The word translated hell in verse 5 is Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem. In the days of the kings of Judah, children were sacrificed there to foreign gods (Jeremiah 7:31), and Jeremiah announced that it would become a valley of slaughter. By Jesus' time Gehenna had become a name for the place of final judgment. Much of this chapter has parallels in Matthew 6, 10, and 24, but the rich fool, the question about the inheritance, and the sayings on fire and baptism are found only in Luke, and the servants waiting for their master partly so.
cultural:
Sparrows were among the cheapest foods in the market. Matthew 10:29 has two sold for a penny (the assarion, a small copper coin worth a fraction of a day's wage), while Luke has five for two pennies, as if one were thrown in for free. Even that one is not forgotten by God.

People often asked respected teachers to arbitrate disputes, and inheritance law (Deuteronomy 21:17) gave an eldest son a double portion, which could leave younger brothers aggrieved. The rich fool's first harvest was a gift of the land, but he speaks only to himself, with no word to God or to neighbors. In an agrarian village, where hoarding grain could drive up prices for the poor, this was more than private foolishness. Night was divided into watches; the second and third were the dead hours in the middle. A master returning from a wedding feast might arrive at any hour. Servants dressed for work tucked their long robes into their belts so they could move freely. In weather lore, a cloud from the west brought rain off the Mediterranean, and a south wind brought heat off the desert.
literary: The chapter is a collection of teaching units joined by catchwords and themes, addressed alternately to the disciples (1-12, 22-53) and to the crowd (13-21, 54-59). Three arguments from lesser to greater (sparrows, ravens, lilies) make the case against fear and anxiety. The parable of the rich fool uses internal monologue, a device Luke's parables use often (15:17-19, 16:3-4, 18:4-5), so that the reader hears the character's heart; then God interrupts the monologue. In the parable of the waiting servants the master astonishingly becomes the servant, dressing himself to serve them at table. Verse 53 draws on Micah 7:6, a lament about a society where even families turn against one another.

outline.t: Fear God, not people; confess the Son of Man
The parable of the rich fool
Do not worry: seek the kingdom

doctrines.note: God feeds the ravens, clothes the lilies, forgets no sparrow, and numbers every hair. His care for his creatures is detailed and personal, and it is the ground for Jesus' command not to fear or worry.
Hidden things will be disclosed, the rich fool's life is required of him, and servants will give account to their returning master. Judgment is proportionate: much is required from those given much.

The Son of Man will come at an unexpected hour. Christian hope is not idle waiting but faithful readiness, and the returning master's promise to serve his servants shows that hope is finally a welcome.

words.note: Pleonexia, greed, literally the desire to have more. Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). Jesus warns against every form of it, because life is not measured by what one owns.
Merimnao, to be anxious or worry. It is the word used of Martha in 10:41. Jesus does not forbid work or planning but the anxious grasping that forgets the Father knows what his children need.

Geenna, Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place of idolatrous child sacrifice in Israel's history, which became a name for final judgment. Jesus uses it to show that God, not human persecutors, holds ultimate authority over life and death.

Oikonomos, a household manager or steward, often a trusted slave put in charge of the master's affairs. Peter's question makes it apply to leaders among the disciples: those given responsibility for others will answer for how they treat them.

christ: Jesus speaks here as the Son of Man who will confess or deny people before the angels of God, and who will come at an hour no one expects. The picture of the master who, finding his servants ready, dresses himself to wait on them at table is a startling image of the Lord's humility; he does exactly this at the Last Supper (22:27), where he says he is among them as one who serves. Jesus also speaks of his own suffering as a baptism he must undergo and of his distress until it is accomplished. The one who tells his disciples not to be afraid is himself going toward the cross with full knowledge, and the kingdom the Father is pleased to give the little flock comes through that baptism.

hard.q: What is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and why can't it be forgiven?
hard.a: Verse 10 has troubled many sensitive readers who fear they have committed it. In Mark 3:28-30 the saying follows the charge that Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul, which suggests that it refers to seeing the Spirit's work in Jesus and deliberately calling it evil. In Luke it sits among warnings about confessing or denying Jesus, and many interpreters read it as a settled, final rejection of the Spirit's testimony to Jesus. Speaking against the Son of Man during his ministry, when his identity was hidden, could be forgiven, as Peter's later denial was; but persistent refusal of the Spirit who reveals Jesus shuts a person off from the very means of forgiveness. It is not unforgivable because God refuses to forgive a repentant sinner, but because this sin refuses repentance. For this reason pastors and theologians have long noted that someone who is anxious about having committed it gives evidence that they have not, since the Spirit is still at work in their conscience.

questions: The rich fool had a good harvest and a reasonable plan. Where exactly did he go wrong, and where are you tempted in the same way?
Jesus tells us to consider the ravens and the lilies. What specific worries would change if you took his argument seriously?
Jesus says much will be required from those given much. What have you been given, and what might be required?
